title: About the translator
html:
About the translator

Kolluru Seetarama Sarma, Smt. Saroja, Chi. Shreyas Sarma

Seetarama Sarma is a seasoned technology professional with decades of experience in leadership roles, including Principal Engineer at AWS and Director of Cloud Engineering at U.S. Bank. A graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, where he earned his Bachelor’s degree in Civil Engineering in 1995, he combines technical expertise with a deep-rooted passion for classical learning.

He holds a Master’s degree in Samskṛtam from the Hindu University of America and comes from a distinguished lineage of Sanskrit scholars. Under the guidance of his father, Sri Kolluru Avatara Sarma—an esteemed teacher of over four decades and author of more than sixty works—he has cultivated a lifelong dedication to the study and preservation of Sanskrit.

title: Foreword
html:
Foreword

There is a sweet history behind bringing 'Ganapati Sambhavam' — this wondrous Sanskrit Mahakavya composed by Mahamahopadhyaya Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri. My revered father, Brahmasri Kolluru Avatara Sarma, was a scholar of the Sanskrit language, a tireless seeker of knowledge, and a devoted man of letters who authored nearly 60 works on Sanatana Dharma. He was my Guru, and the root inspiration for this sacred undertaking. He was a great devotee of Ganesha who had himself translated the 'Mudgala Purana' — dedicated specifically to the worship of Ganesha — into Telugu. While reading the 'Ganesha Upasanank' published by Gita Press, he had noticed the humorous conversation between Ganapati and Parashurama quoted there from 'Ganapati Sambhavam', and he would often bring up those verses with us.

He searched for this rare work for many years. About two years ago, at his request, I searched for this text and learned that it was available at the 'Michigan State University Library' in America. Fortunately, my friend Sri Palli Venkata Subbaraya Sarma took great pains to procure this text through his son Sattvik Sarma and sent it to me.

After reading this work and coming to appreciate the immense literary treasures and wondrous episodes within it, my joy knew no bounds. This translated volume is my humble attempt, born of the earnest wish to offer this most sacred and singular Mahakavya, in our mother tongue of Telugu, to devotees of Ganesha and to connoisseurs who delight in Sanskrit literature.

This effort, undertaken for the joy of the soul (svāntaḥsukham) and for the welfare of the world, has employed artificial intelligence merely as a tool. I consider it to have served as a bridge between the vast treasury of knowledge left by the ancient masters and my own modest curiosity.

By the grace of Sri Ganesha, I hope this labor will be of some benefit to devotees. May all of this be an offering at the lotus feet of Sri Mahaganapati!

Yours,

Kolluru Seetarama Sarma

title: The Poet
html:
The Poet

Sri Prabhudatta Shastri, 1892–1979

Among the great Mahakavyas to emerge in modern Sanskrit literature, 'Ganapati Sambhavam' holds a place of honor. This wondrous work of ten sargas, composed in the spirit of the ancient Mahakavi Kalidasa's 'Kumarasambhavam', was written by that crest-jewel among poets — Mahamahopadhyaya, Vidya-Vachaspati Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri.

Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri was born into the illustrious Mishra lineage, in a village called 'Tatarpur' west of the town of Alwar in the state of Rajasthan. His great-grandfather was Pandit Shaligrama Mishra, a great scholar who wrote commentaries on the Srimad Bhagavatam and other texts, and who copied out the Valmiki Ramayana with his own hand.

His grandfather was Sri Ramapratapa Mishra, a great benefactor who offered Ayurvedic medical care to the people free of charge, without expecting any fee; the local people, pleased with his service, lovingly called him 'Lattu Mishra'. His father was Sri Ramasharana Mishra. Shastri-ji was born in the Vikrama year 1946 (1892 CE), on Phalguna Shukla Panchami, a Thursday. When he was but two years old, his father passed into the eternal abode, and he was raised in the care of his compassionate mother and his grandfather.

For his education, he was sent to a town called 'Mandawa' in the Marwar region. There he studied all the shastras under teachers named Pandit Vilasaram Shukla, Mohan Lal, and Suryananda. He later moved to the city of Delhi, where he taught as a schoolteacher and earned great fame and renown.

His profound scholarship won him many prestigious honors. At the special Gita-artha competitions held at Kurukshetra, under the patronage of the Prime Minister of Patiala, Dyaliram, he secured first place — in resolving apparent contradictions among commentaries on the Gita — and won the 'Gold Medal'. At the All-India Sanskrit Literary Conference held in Patna, he composed a marvelous samasya-purti (extemporaneous completion of a verse) on the word 'Sanskritam' and received the title 'Sarvottama Kavi' (Best of Poets).

Alongside this Mahakavya 'Ganapati Sambhavam', Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri composed many other rare works in the Sanskrit language. A list of those works:

Srimad Bhagavad Gita Vyangya Mandakini (a commentary)
Virata Rupa Darshanam
Dhanvantari Janmamritam
Gandhi Nandi Shraddhamritam and Charakha Vandanamritam
Samskrita Vagvijayamu (a play)
Samskrita Vak Saundaryamritam
Rashtradhwajamritam
Jhansiswari Shauryamritam
Mahimna Stotram (with a Hindi commentary)
Mahalakshmi Puja

Without abandoning the conventions of classical poetic composition, Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri was a rare and innovative craftsman who wove modern nationalist sentiments, the spirit of India's freedom struggle, the valor of Jhansi Lakshmibai, Mahatma Gandhi's charkha, and the national flag into Sanskrit verse. His compositions, appearing as they do in the modern age, are priceless ornaments bestowed upon the Sanskrit language.

title: Ganapati Sambhavam — An Introduction to This Wondrous Mahakavya
html:
Ganapati Sambhavam — An Introduction to This Wondrous Mahakavya

We are all well acquainted with the Mahakavya 'Kumarasambhavam', composed by the great poet Kalidasa. If the younger brother Kumaraswami has so great an epic devoted to him, how fitting would it be if the elder brother Ganapati — foremost among those worthy of worship — also had a Mahakavya of his own? That very wondrous thought was the seed from which Mahamahopadhyaya Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri's Mahakavya 'Ganapati Sambhavam' arose! This work of ten sargas is not confined merely to the flavor of devotion (Bhakti-rasa); it weaves in modern social ideas as well, offering readers a fresh and invigorating experience.

This poetic journey begins delightfully with a description of the natural beauty of the snow-capped Himalayas, Kashmir, and Nepal. The wedding of Shiva and Parvati, and thereafter Parvati Devi breathing life into a clay figure through her yogic power to create Ganapati, are described most wondrously. When the boy, standing guard at his mother's command, obstructs none other than Shiva himself as he returns home — the ensuing logical debate (Shastrartha) between the two over the question "Who is a father?" holds the reader spellbound.

Thereafter, the humorous war of words between Ganapati and Parashurama, in which he loses one tusk and becomes 'Ekadanta' (the one-tusked), unfolds with great zest. Likewise, Ganapati's swift writing of the Mahabharata alongside Veda Vyasa, and his winning — through sheer cleverness — of the divine 'modaka' (sweet dumpling) offered by the gods, by circling his parents in competition with Kumaraswami, bring forth much laughter.

The most fascinating episode in this Mahakavya is its comparison of Ganapati's very form to the modern ideal of 'Democracy'! The poet explains how a leader with large ears and small eyes ought to be — one who listens closely to the people's words while observing with subtle discernment. That the poet should apply modern national ideals — equal rights for all people, equality between man and woman, the eradication of poverty, and religious harmony — to the very form of Ganapati is testament to his boundless intellect.

While relishing the style of classical poetry, this is a wondrous Mahakavya that everyone wishing to witness a blend of devotion, logic, humor, nationalism, and modern political thought must read without fail!

title: A Comparative Study with Kalidasa's Kumarasambhavam
html:
A Comparative Study with Kalidasa's Kumarasambhavam

In Sanskrit literature, the Mahakavya 'Kumarasambhavam', composed by the great poet Kalidasa, occupies a place without parallel. Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri's modern Mahakavya 'Ganapati Sambhavam' is a wondrous continuation of that ancient poetic tradition. When these two Mahakavyas are examined comparatively, with a scholar's eye, one clearly sees both the episodes in which Shastri-ji follows in Kalidasa's footsteps, and the variations in which he weaves in his own independent, modern, and secular ideas.

Episodes Inspired by Kalidasa

The Kavya's Invocation — Description of the Himalayas

It is notable that both Mahakavyas begin with a description of the Himalaya mountain.

Where Kalidasa describes the Himalayas as the very soul of the gods, a measuring-rod for the earth —

अस्त्युत्तरस्यां दिशि देवतात्मा हिमालयो नाम नगाधिराजः ।
astyuttarasyāṃ diśi devatātmā himālayo nāma nagādhirājaḥ |
पूर्वापरौ तोयनिधी वगाह्य स्थितः पृथिव्या इव मानदंडः ॥
pūrvāparau toyanidhī vagāhya sthitaḥ pṛthivyā iva mānadaṃḍaḥ ||

— Kumarasambhavam

Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri describes the Himalayas as an aged Indian elder, wearing a white turban, standing guard over the northern direction —

अस्त्यत्रोत्तरदिक्-सुरक्षणचणः, शैलो हिमानी-धनी
astyatrottaradik-surakṣaṇacaṇaḥ, śailo himānī-dhanī
श्वेतोष्णीषधरेषु भारतवयोवृद्धेषु मन्येऽग्रणीः ।
śvetoṣṇīṣadhareṣu bhāratavayovṛddheṣu manye'graṇīḥ |
व्यक्तोऽस्येव किरीटवत् 'स्फटिक' इत्याख्यः सितांशुर्मणिः
vyakto'syeva kirīṭavat 'sphaṭika' ityākhyaḥ sitāṃśurmaṇiḥ
तेनैवाऽस्य यशस्ततान भुवनेऽभूत् कालिदासोऽनृणी ॥
tenaivā'sya yaśastatāna bhuvane'bhūt kālidāso'nṛṇī ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

The Birth of Parvati

The birth of Jagadamba Parvati Devi in the womb of Menaka, wife of the Himalayas, is described most beautifully in both Mahakavyas. Shastri-ji, too, clearly states that the same goddess who had been Sati Devi in her former birth was reborn as Menaka's daughter.

प्रसन्नदिक्पांसुविविक्तवातं शंखस्वनानंतरपुष्पवृष्टि ।
prasannadikpāṃsuviviktavātaṃ śaṃkhasvanānaṃtarapuṣpavṛṣṭi |
शरीरिणां स्थावरजंगमानां सुखाय तज्जन्मदिनं बभूव ॥
śarīriṇāṃ sthāvarajaṃgamānāṃ sukhāya tajjanmadinaṃ babhūva ||

— Kumarasambhavam

'मेनैणी' नयनी स्व-कुक्षि पटलात् कन्याऽऽख्यरत्नं ददे ।
'menaiṇī' nayanī sva-kukṣi paṭalāt kanyā''khyaratnaṃ dade |
सौभाग्याभिध रत्नदान निपुणं कन्यांतरेभ्योऽपि यत् ॥
saubhāgyābhidha ratnadāna nipuṇaṃ kanyāṃtarebhyo'pi yat ||
आसीद् दक्षसुता स्वपूर्व जनने ख्याता 'सती' नामतः ।
āsīd dakṣasutā svapūrva janane khyātā 'satī' nāmataḥ |
सैवाऽद्यावि रभूद् गिरींद्रसदने ज्योतिस्तति र्जंगमा ॥
saivā'dyāvi rabhūd girīṃdrasadane jyotistati rjaṃgamā ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

The Meaning of the Name 'Aparna'

The poet has drawn directly from the Kumarasambhavam the episode of Parvati Devi's severe austerity — undertaken to win Parameshvara Shiva as her husband — in which she abstained even from eating leaves, and thereby earned the name 'Aparna' (she who ate not even a leaf).

स्वयं विशीर्णद्रुमपर्णवृत्तिता परा हि काष्ठा तपसस्तया पुनः ।
svayaṃ viśīrṇadrumaparṇavṛttitā parā hi kāṣṭhā tapasastayā punaḥ |
तदप्यपाकीर्णमतः प्रियंवदां अपर्णेति च तां पुराविदः ॥
tadapyapākīrṇamataḥ priyaṃvadāṃ aparṇeti ca tāṃ purāvidaḥ ||

— Kumarasambhavam

लब्धुं या शिव माद नैव तपसि प्राप्तं च पर्णं तरोः ।
labdhuṃ yā śiva māda naiva tapasi prāptaṃ ca parṇaṃ taroḥ |
कर्णार्कार्ण समेतसद्‌गुणचयं चंद्रावतंसाऽह्वयम् ॥
karṇārkārṇa sametasad‌guṇacayaṃ caṃdrāvataṃsā'hvayam ||
तेनापीह मतेव या यतिवरै वृक्षादिपत्राऽऽशनैः ।
tenāpīha mateva yā yativarai vṛkṣādipatrā''śanaiḥ |
अभ्यर्णस्थसुवर्ण लज्जनकरी क्रांत्याख्यकांत्या युता ॥
abhyarṇasthasuvarṇa lajjanakarī krāṃtyākhyakāṃtyā yutā ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

Parameshvara Shiva's Yogic Samadhi

Shiva entering into deep meditation upon the Himalayan peaks, fixing his gaze between the eyebrows, and practicing pranayama, is drawn entirely from Kalidasa's descriptions. Shastri-ji has wondrously described the hearing of the 'So'ham' sound within the breath.

पर्यंकबंधस्थिरपूर्वकायं ऋज्वायतं सन्नमितोभयांसम् ।
paryaṃkabaṃdhasthirapūrvakāyaṃ ṛjvāyataṃ sannamitobhayāṃsam |
उत्तानपाणिद्वयसन्निवेशात् प्रफुल्लराजीवमिवांकमध्ये ॥
uttānapāṇidvayasanniveśāt praphullarājīvamivāṃkamadhye ||

— Kumarasambhavam

प्राणयामपरै रवैक्षि विमलो 'हं' 'सो' निजश्वासयोः ।
prāṇayāmaparai ravaikṣi vimalo 'haṃ' 'so' nijaśvāsayoḥ |
आगच्छत्प्रतिगच्छतो र्ध्वनिकरो निश्चंचुपत्पक्षकः ॥
āgacchatpratigacchato rdhvanikaro niścaṃcupatpakṣakaḥ ||
ये चिन्वंति सुमौक्तिकेन सदृशान् श्वासान् प्रकाशान्वितान् ।
ye cinvaṃti sumauktikena sadṛśān śvāsān prakāśānvitān |
ते हंसाः परमाः सुचिन्मयसरस्वत्याः प्रिया वाहनाः ॥
te haṃsāḥ paramāḥ sucinmayasarasvatyāḥ priyā vāhanāḥ ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

The Great Festival of the Bestowal of the Bride

Just as the Kumarasambhavam describes the bride and groom joining hands, so too Pandit Prabhudatta-ji, in the episode of the giving away of the bride (Kanyadana), most naturally likens a daughter's passage from her father's lineage to her husband's lineage to the river Ganga leaving her place of birth to reach the ocean.

तस्याः करं वड्रमुखो मुखेन व्याकंपमानांगुलिमाजघाम । …
tasyāḥ karaṃ vaḍramukho mukhena vyākaṃpamānāṃgulimājaghāma | …

— Kumarasambhavam

तस्मादस्य करेऽर्ण्यतां जलमिदं पत्यैव संबंधकृत् ।
tasmādasya kare'rṇyatāṃ jalamidaṃ patyaiva saṃbaṃdhakṛt |
गंगायाःसलिलं यथोद्गमभुवं त्यक्त्वैति भूम्यंतरम् ॥
gaṃgāyāḥsalilaṃ yathodgamabhuvaṃ tyaktvaiti bhūmyaṃtaram ||
गंगा शीर्षधृता करोति शपथाचारान् दृढान् सन्नृणाम् ।
gaṃgā śīrṣadhṛtā karoti śapathācārān dṛḍhān sannṛṇām |
साऽप्येतेन धृताऽधुना तदभयत् पाणिग्रहोऽयं दृढः ॥
sā'pyetena dhṛtā'dhunā tadabhayat pāṇigraho'yaṃ dṛḍhaḥ ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

Novel Departures in the Ganapati Sambhavam

While honoring the ancient poetic tradition, Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri wove in contemporary social, political, and national realities, creating a new style altogether distinct from Kalidasa's.

Contemporary Geographical Descriptions (Kashmir, Nepal)

Where Kalidasa described only the mythic Himalaya, Shastri-ji describes Kashmir as the very chest of the Himalayas and Nepal as its head, in the most vivid and modern geographical terms. The poet notes that Kashmir, famed for its saffron, remains dear to us even though it has suffered the ravages of demonic raiders.

काश्मीरेति पदाभिधं गिरिपते र्वक्षोऽक्षिलक्ष्यम् जनैः ।
kāśmīreti padābhidhaṃ giripate rvakṣo'kṣilakṣyam janaiḥ |
रक्षस्तक्षणभक्षणक्षय मितं किंचित् तथापि प्रियम् ॥
rakṣastakṣaṇabhakṣaṇakṣaya mitaṃ kiṃcit tathāpi priyam ||

— Description of Kashmir, Ganapati Sambhavam

नेपालोऽस्य गिरे र्ललाट तट-भः प्राशस्त्य-भूयस्त्ववान् ।
nepālo'sya gire rlalāṭa taṭa-bhaḥ prāśastya-bhūyastvavān |
कस्तूरी मृगबंधुरः प्रतिवनं घ्रातुंच मित्राणि यम् ॥
kastūrī mṛgabaṃdhuraḥ prativanaṃ ghrātuṃca mitrāṇi yam ||

— Description of Nepal, Ganapati Sambhavam

Modern Weapons of Defense (Tanks and Bombs)

The poet's bold and startling independent invention is his introduction, into this classical Mahakavya, of modern weapons unknown in Kalidasa's time — tanks, bombs, and guns — in his description of the Indian soldiers standing guard over the Himalayas.

'वारूदं' च कृपीटयोनिजननं तद्-गोपकं 'बम्' च यत् ।
'vārūdaṃ' ca kṛpīṭayonijananaṃ tad-gopakaṃ 'bam' ca yat |
यत्-पार्श्वे शयनं करोति सखिवत् जागर्ति संकेततः ॥
yat-pārśve śayanaṃ karoti sakhivat jāgarti saṃketataḥ ||
"'टांकान्' वक्रमुखान् शशांकसदृशान् नूत्नान् नवांकांश्च वा ।
"'ṭāṃkān' vakramukhān śaśāṃkasadṛśān nūtnān navāṃkāṃśca vā |
कारंकार मिमे हसंति कपिवत् लंकाविटंकान् यथा ॥
kāraṃkāra mime hasaṃti kapivat laṃkāviṭaṃkān yathā ||

— Bombs and Tanks, Ganapati Sambhavam

The Creation of Ganapati from Clay through Yogic Power

Where Kumaraswami's birth proceeds through Shiva's radiance, by way of Agni, the Ganga, and the Krittikas, Ganapati is instead created by Parvati Devi from the natural residue of her own body, into which she breathes life through her yogic power — an entirely different method, which the poet defends not as mere Puranic legend but as a wondrous feat of yogic science.

सा सम्मृद्य मृदं स्वशुद्धिरसिका कृत्वा च तद्धृतकाम् ।
sā sammṛdya mṛdaṃ svaśuddhirasikā kṛtvā ca taddhṛtakām |
ऐच्छ त्ता मपरत्र कुत्रचिदपि प्रक्षेप्तु मुद्यत्पदा ॥
aiccha ttā maparatra kutracidapi prakṣeptu mudyatpadā ||
संयोज्याऽपर्मृत्स्नया रज इदं कृत्वेव तत् पुष्कलम् ।
saṃyojyā'parmṛtsnayā raja idaṃ kṛtveva tat puṣkalam |
स्वाखं पुच्छकमुच्छतोऽतिललितं गिर्यात्मजा निर्ममे ॥
svākhaṃ pucchakamucchato'tilalitaṃ giryātmajā nirmame ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

The Metaphor of Democratic Governance

The ninth sarga of this Mahakavya is the most revolutionary passage in the history of Sanskrit literature. The poet's comparison of Ganapati's very bodily form to modern democratic governance is a mark of his extraordinary vision. He defines the true 'Ganashasana' (rule of the Ganas) as governance that wins the goodwill of the people without mutual violence or corruption.

यन्न स्याद् रणतंत्र मेव च मिथो मुष्टिप्रहारप्रियम् ।
yanna syād raṇataṃtra meva ca mitho muṣṭiprahārapriyam |
न स्यान्मुष्टिकरं समागतजनग्रंथिस्थवित्तस्य वा ॥
na syānmuṣṭikaraṃ samāgatajanagraṃthisthavittasya vā ||
चेतस्तुष्टिकरं सुपुष्टिकरणं स्नेहस्य देहस्य वा ।
cetastuṣṭikaraṃ supuṣṭikaraṇaṃ snehasya dehasya vā |
तत् प्रोक्तं गणशासनाऽपर पदं गाजाननं शासनम् ॥
tat proktaṃ gaṇaśāsanā'para padaṃ gājānanaṃ śāsanam ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

Description of the National Flag

In the first sarga, in describing the Himalayas — red with flowers, green with trees, and white with snow — the poet observes that these mountain ranges themselves evoke India's national tricolor flag. This is a striking departure entirely absent from classical Sanskrit Mahakavyas, and stands as testament to the poet's boundless patriotism.

पुष्पैःशोणतमो द्रुमैश्च हरितः श्वेत स्तुषारैश्च यः ।
puṣpaiḥśoṇatamo drumaiśca haritaḥ śveta stuṣāraiśca yaḥ |
नानाऽऽक्रामकवातघातकुशलोऽद्रिस्कंधसंबंधवान् ॥
nānā''krāmakavātaghātakuśalo'driskaṃdhasaṃbaṃdhavān ||
तोयांतःस्थ सरोजिनीमयमहामालादलाऽऽलिंगितः ।
toyāṃtaḥstha sarojinīmayamahāmālādalā''liṃgitaḥ |
हं हो !! भारत राष्ट्रसद्ध्वजविभा मालिंगती वांगतः ॥
haṃ ho !! bhārata rāṣṭrasaddhvajavibhā māliṃgatī vāṃgataḥ ||

— Ganapati Sambhavam

If Kalidasa's 'Kumarasambhavam' stands as a sacred foundation for Sanskrit literature, then Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri's 'Ganapati Sambhavam' is the modern temple devotedly built atop that very foundation. Without abandoning classical poetic conventions, and while nourishing Kalidasa's own poetic flavors, Pandit Prabhudatta Shastri is a rare craftsman who shaped modern nationalist sentiment, the spirit of India's freedom struggle, and modern political thought into Sanskrit verse. There can be no doubt that this work is a golden bridge between the ancient and the modern.

title: Dedication
html:
Dedication

दिष्ट्या ! सम्भवकारकं गणपतेः काव्यं प्रकाशं गतम् ।
diṣṭyā ! sambhavakārakaṃ gaṇapateḥ kāvyaṃ prakāśaṃ gatam |
तद्गृह्णन्तु शिवा शिवो गणपतिः स्कन्दः सनन्दीगणः ॥
tadgṛhṇantu śivā śivo gaṇapatiḥ skandaḥ sanandīgaṇaḥ ||
व्यासो भारत-भा-विभासनकरः श्रीकालिदासादयः ।
vyāso bhārata-bhā-vibhāsanakaraḥ śrīkālidāsādayaḥ |
नेपालस्य धराधरा 'वर'-धरा-शोणाऽधरश्रीधवाः ॥ 1 ॥
nepālasya dharādharā 'vara'-dharā-śoṇā'dharaśrīdhavāḥ || 1 ||
Anvaya

दिष्ट्या! गणपतेः सम्भवकारकम् काव्यम् प्रकाशम् गतम्. तत् शिवा शिवः गणपतिः स्कन्दः सनन्दीगणः, भारत-भा-विभासनकरः व्यासः, श्रीकालिदासादयः, नेपालस्य धराधराः, 'वर'-धरा-शोणाऽधरश्रीधवाः गृह्णन्तु.

Word Meanings
दिष्ट्या = by great good fortune (a most joyous thing)
गणपतेः = of Ganapati
सम्भवकारकम् = (सम्भवं करोति इति — upapada compound) that which brings about the birth
काव्यम् = this Mahakavya
प्रकाशम् = publication (into the light)
गतम् = has attained
तत् = that (this Kavya)
शिवा = Goddess Parvati
शिवः = Parameshvara Shiva
गणपतिः = Ganapati
स्कन्दः = Kumaraswami
सनन्दीगणः = (नन्दिना सहितः गणः — sahita bahuvrīhi) the retinue of Shiva together with Nandishvara
भारत-भा-विभासनकरः = (भारतस्य भा, भारतभा, तस्याः विभासनं करोति इति — upapada compound) he who causes the splendor of the Mahabharata to shine forth
व्यासः = Maharishi Vyasa
श्रीकालिदासादयः = (श्रीकालिदासः आदिः येषां ते — bahuvrīhi compound) Sri Kalidasa and other great poets
नेपालस्य = of the land of Nepal
धराधराः = those who rule the earth (kings)
'वर'-धरा-शोणाऽधरश्रीधवाः = (वराणां धरा, तस्याः शोणाः अधराः, तेषां श्रीः, तस्याः धवाः — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) 'Vara' means saffron; the Indians who are lords of the splendor of the red lips of the land of Kashmir, where it is grown
गृह्णन्तु = may they graciously accept!
Meaning

It is a matter of the greatest joy that this Mahakavya, which brings about the birth of Ganapati, has now come into publication. May it be accepted by Shiva and Parvati, by Ganapati, by Kumaraswami and the retinue of Shiva together with Nandishvara; likewise by Maharishi Vyasa, who caused the splendor of the Mahabharata to shine before the world, and by Kalidasa and other great poets; by the kings who rule the land of Nepal; and by the people of India, lords of the splendor of the red lips of the land of Kashmir, where saffron is grown!

ग्रन्थो भारत नामको गणपते ! श्रीमत्करोल्लेखितः ।
grantho bhārata nāmako gaṇapate ! śrīmatkarollekhitaḥ |
काव्यं लाघववत्ततः पुनरिदं रोचिष्यते किं च ते ? ॥
kāvyaṃ lāghavavattataḥ punaridaṃ rociṣyate kiṃ ca te ? ||
किन्तु त्वं मनसि स्थित श्चिरतमात् कालान् मुहुः प्रेरयः ।
kintu tvaṃ manasi sthita ściratamāt kālān muhuḥ prerayaḥ |
तत्स्वप्रेरणगौरवस्मरणतो ऽवश्यं तव स्तात् प्रियम् ॥ 2 ॥
tatsvapreraṇagauravasmaraṇato 'vaśyaṃ tava stāt priyam || 2 ||
Anvaya

हे गणपते! भारतनामकः ग्रन्थः श्रीमत्करोल्लेखितः. ततः पुनः लाघववत् इदम् काव्यम् ते किम् च रोचिष्यते? किन्तु त्वम् चिरतमात् कालात् मनसि स्थितः (सन्) मुहुः प्रेरयः. तत् स्वप्रेरणगौरवस्मरणतः तव अवश्यम् प्रियम् स्तात्.

Word Meanings
गणपते = O Ganapati!
भारतनामकः = (भारतं नाम यस्य सः — bahuvrīhi compound) known by the name Mahabharata
ग्रन्थः = the great scripture
श्रीमत्करोल्लेखितः = (श्रीमता करेण उल्लेखितः — tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa) written by your own auspicious hand
ततः = than that
लाघववत् = far smaller
इदम् = this
काव्यम् = Kavya
पुनः = again
ते = to you
किम् च = would it at all
रोचिष्यते = be pleasing?
किन्तु = but
त्वम् = you
चिरतमात् = for a very long
कालात् = time
मनसि = in my mind
स्थितः = having remained
मुहुः = again and again
प्रेरयः = urged (me to write it)
तत् = therefore
स्वप्रेरणगौरवस्मरणतः = (स्वस्य प्रेरणस्य गौरवस्य स्मरणतः — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) by remembering the honor of your own urging
तव = to you
अवश्यम् = surely
प्रियम् = dear
स्तात् = may it become.
Meaning

O Ganapati! A great scripture such as the Mahabharata itself was written by your own sacred hand. Would this Kavya, so much smaller than that, be pleasing to you at all? And yet, you have dwelt in my mind for a very long time, repeatedly urging me to write it. Therefore, in remembrance of the honor of your own urging, this will surely be dear to you.

देवा भक्तिपरीक्षका इति चिरादुद्घोष्यते कोविदैः ।
devā bhaktiparīkṣakā iti cirādudghoṣyate kovidaiḥ |
तन्नो वस्तुविशेषलाघवगुरुत्वाकाङ्क्षका स्त्वादृशाः ॥
tanno vastuviśeṣalāghavagurutvākāṅkṣakā stvādṛśāḥ ||
कस्तूरीजननक्षमोऽपि हरिणो गृह्णाति पुष्पोद्भवम् ।
kastūrījananakṣamo'pi hariṇo gṛhṇāti puṣpodbhavam |
गन्धं दीनदयाम्बुधे ! मम हठाद् ग्राह्यं त्वया ऽपीदकम् ॥ 3 ॥
gandhaṃ dīnadayāmbudhe ! mama haṭhād grāhyaṃ tvayā 'pīdakam || 3 ||
Anvaya

देवाः भक्तिपरीक्षकाः इति चिरात् कोविदैः उद्घोष्यते. तत् त्वादृशाः वस्तुविशेषलाघवगुरुत्वाकाङ्क्षकाः नो (सन्ति). कस्तूरीजननक्षमः अपि हरिणः पुष्पोद्भवम् गन्धम् गृह्णाति. दीनदयाम्बुधे! मम हठात् त्वया अपि इदकम् ग्राह्यम्.

Word Meanings
देवाः = the gods
भक्तिपरीक्षकाः = (भक्तेः परीक्षकाः — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) testers of devotion
इति = thus
चिरात् = since ancient times
कोविदैः = by the learned
उद्घोष्यते = it is proclaimed
तत् = therefore
त्वादृशाः = those like you
वस्तुविशेषलाघवगुरुत्वाकाङ्क्षकाः = (वस्तूनां विशेषः, तस्य लाघवं च गुरुत्वं च, तयोः आकाङ्क्षकाः — dvandva-embedded ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) those who care whether an offered thing is grand or small
नो = are not
कस्तूरीजननक्षमः = (कस्तूर्याः जनने क्षमः — saptamī tatpuruṣa) though capable of producing fragrant musk itself
अपि = even
हरिणः = the deer
पुष्पोद्भवम् = (पुष्पात् उद्भवः यस्य तम् — bahuvrīhi) arising from a flower
गन्धम् = fragrance
गृह्णाति = does indeed accept
दीनदयाम्बुधे = (दीनेषु दया, तस्याः अम्बुधिः, तत्सम्बुद्धिः) O Lord, ocean of compassion for the humble!
मम = my
हठात् = out of sheer insistence
त्वया अपि = by you too
इदकम् = this small Kavya
ग्राह्यम् = is to be accepted.
Meaning

The learned have long proclaimed that the gods test only the devotion of their devotees. Hence, gods such as yourself do not care whether the offering presented is small or great. Even the deer, itself capable of producing the fragrant musk, still delights in the fragrance of a forest flower! In the same way, O ocean of compassion for the humble, though you are the abode of the Vedas and of great Mahakavyas, you must accept this small offering that I press upon you with such insistence.

ग्रन्थोल्लेखक एव लेखनकृतां जानाति लेखश्रमम् ।
granthollekhaka eva lekhanakṛtāṃ jānāti lekhaśramam |
किं जानाति च वेदनां प्रसवजां वन्ध्या कदाचित् क्वचित् ॥
kiṃ jānāti ca vedanāṃ prasavajāṃ vandhyā kadācit kvacit ||
श्रीमानेव ततोऽवधारिततमो वर्ण्यः समर्प्योऽपि वा ।
śrīmāneva tato'vadhāritatamo varṇyaḥ samarpyo'pi vā |
तत् त्वं मोदकतुल्य मात्मचरितं गृह्णीष्व मल्लेखितम् ॥ 4 ॥
tat tvaṃ modakatulya mātmacaritaṃ gṛhṇīṣva mallekhitam || 4 ||
Anvaya

ग्रन्थोल्लेखकः एव लेखनकृताम् लेखश्रमम् जानाति. वन्ध्या क्वचित् कदाचित् प्रसवजाम् वेदनाम् किम् जानाति च? ततः श्रीमान् एव वर्ण्यः समर्प्यः अपि वा अवधारिततमः. तत् त्वम् मोदकतुल्यम् मल्लेखितम् आत्मचरितम् गृह्णीष्व.

Word Meanings
ग्रन्थोल्लेखकः = (ग्रन्थस्य उल्लेखकः — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) one who has written a great scripture
एव = alone
लेखनकृताम् = (लेखनं कुर्वन्ति इति तेषाम् — upapada compound) of scribes who undertake the labor of writing
लेखश्रमम् = the toil of writing
जानाति = can know
वन्ध्या = a barren woman
क्वचित् = anywhere
कदाचित् = at any time
प्रसवजाम् = (प्रसवात् जाता, ताम् — pañcamī tatpuruṣa) born of childbirth
वेदनाम् = the pain
किम् जानाति च = can she know at all? (she cannot)
ततः = therefore
श्रीमान् एव = you alone, the illustrious one (who wrote out the Vyasa-Bharata)
वर्ण्यः = worthy of being praised
समर्प्यः अपि वा = and also worthy of being offered this dedication
अवधारिततमः = have been resolved upon by me
तत् = therefore
त्वम् = you
मोदकतुल्यम् = (मोदकेन तुल्यम् — tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa) sweet as a modaka
मल्लेखितम् = (मया लेखितम् — tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa) written by me
आत्मचरितम् = (आत्मनः चरितम् — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) this account of your own life
गृह्णीष्व = please accept.
Meaning

Only one who has himself written a great scripture can know the toil that scribes undergo in writing. Can a barren woman ever know the pain of childbirth? Since you yourself once wrote out the Mahabharata, only you can truly know that toil — and so I have resolved that you alone are worthy both of being praised in this work and of receiving its dedication. Therefore, please accept this account of your own life, written by me, sweet as a modaka.

किञ्च ख्याति मिता चिराच्च भवतः खण्डे गुडस्यापि यत् ।
kiñca khyāti mitā cirācca bhavataḥ khaṇḍe guḍasyāpi yat |
लालां मुञ्चति लालसावशगता जिह्वाऽलसत्यागिनी ॥
lālāṃ muñcati lālasāvaśagatā jihvā'lasatyāginī ||
तत् स्वान्तं मम शान्तिचुम्बनकरं स्यादेव तेऽदः प्रियम् ।
tat svāntaṃ mama śānticumbanakaraṃ syādeva te'daḥ priyam |
भक्तानां हठपूरके त्वयि च वा कः संशयो जायते ? ॥ 5 ॥
bhaktānāṃ haṭhapūrake tvayi ca vā kaḥ saṃśayo jāyate ? || 5 ||
Anvaya

किञ्च चिरात् ख्यातिम् इता यत् गुडस्य खण्डे अपि भवतः जिह्वा अलसत्यागिनी (सती) लालसावशगता लालाम् मुञ्चति. तत् मम स्वान्तम् शान्तिचुम्बनकरम्. (तर्हि) अदः ते प्रियम् स्यात् एव. च वा भक्तानाम् हठपूरके त्वयि कः संशयः जायते?

Word Meanings
किञ्च = and, moreover
चिरात् = since long ago
ख्यातिम् इता = has become famous, has it not
यत् = that
गुडस्य खण्डे अपि = even at the mere sight of a piece of jaggery
भवतः = your
जिह्वा = tongue
अलसत्यागिनी = casting off all sloth
लालसावशगता = (लालसायाः वशं गता — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) overcome by intense craving
लालाम् = saliva
मुञ्चति = begins to flow
तत् = that very fact
मम स्वान्तम् = my own heart
शान्तिचुम्बनकरम् = (शान्त्याः चुम्बनं करोति इति — upapada compound) fills with the kiss of tranquility (soothes it deeply)
(तर्हि) अदः = therefore this (offering)
ते = to you
प्रियम् स्यात् एव = will surely be dear
च वा = and moreover
भक्तानाम् = of devotees
हठपूरके = the fulfiller of insistent wishes
त्वयि = in you
कः संशयः = what doubt
जायते = can arise? (none at all).
Meaning

It has long been famous that the mere sight of a piece of jaggery makes your tongue, casting off all sloth, overcome with craving and begin to water. That very fact fills my own heart with deep tranquility. For if you crave even a simple piece of jaggery, then this offering of mine — however small, made with such labor and devotion — will surely be dear to you as well. And when you are the very one who fulfills the insistent wishes of your devotees, what doubt can there possibly be that you will accept it!

बालानामपि पुस्तकाननगतं स्वं नाम पश्यन् भवान् ।
bālānāmapi pustakānanagataṃ svaṃ nāma paśyan bhavān |
तत् कल्याणततिं तनोति हसता स्वास्येन लास्येन वा ॥
tat kalyāṇatatiṃ tanoti hasatā svāsyena lāsyena vā ||
तत् तावकपुस्तकं चरिततः निर्माणतो मामकम् ।
tat tāvakapustakaṃ caritataḥ nirmāṇato māmakam |
दृष्ट्वा नैव करिष्यसि सुविततश्रीवृद्दिसिद्ध्यालयम् ॥ 6 ॥
dṛṣṭvā naiva kariṣyasi suvitataśrīvṛddisiddhyālayam || 6 ||
Anvaya

भवान् बालानाम् पुस्तकाननगतम् अपि स्वम् नाम पश्यन्, हसता स्वास्येन लास्येन वा तत् कल्याणततिम् तनोति. तत् चरिततः तावकपुस्तकम्, निर्माणतः मामकम् दृष्ट्वा (इदम् पुस्तकम्) सुविततश्रीवृद्दिसिद्ध्यालयम् न एव करिष्यसि (किम्)?

Word Meanings
भवान् = you
बालानाम् = of children
पुस्तकाननगतम् अपि = (पुस्तकस्य आननं, तत्र गतम् — saptamī tatpuruṣa) even when it appears merely on the cover, or first page, of their schoolbooks
स्वम् नाम = your own name (the writing of "Śrī Gaṇeśāya Namaḥ")
पश्यन् = upon seeing
हसता = with a smiling
स्वास्येन = (स्वस्य आस्यम्, तेन — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) face of your own, or
लास्येन वा = with a dance
तत् कल्याणततिम् = (कल्याणानां ततिः, ताम् — ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) that abundance of blessings for those children
तनोति = you cause to spread, do you not
तत् = that being so
चरिततः = as regards its story (subject-matter)
तावकपुस्तकम् = this book of yours
निर्माणतः = as regards its making (composition)
मामकम् = this book of mine
दृष्ट्वा = upon seeing
सुविततश्रीवृद्दिसिद्ध्यालयम् = (सुवितता च असौ श्रीश्च, वृद्धिश्च, सिद्धिश्च, तासाम् आलयम् — karmadhāraya, dvandva, ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa) an abode of vast prosperity, growth, and success
न एव करिष्यसि (किम्) = will you not make it so? (surely you will).
Meaning

When children merely see your name — written as "Śrī Gaṇeśāya Namaḥ" — on the very first page of their schoolbooks, you spread abundant blessings upon them, whether smiling with your own face or dancing your joyous dance! That being so, upon seeing this book — yours in its subject-matter, and mine in its making — will you not make it, too, an abode of vast prosperity, growth, and success? Surely you will.

title: A Brief Preface
html:
A Brief Preface

Kavya-shastra (the science of poetics) is the third, blissful form among the sat-chit-ananda aspects of the Supreme Brahman. It is for this very reason that scholars call it Shabda-Brahman (the Word as Brahman). The saying "kāvya śāstra vinodena kālo gacchati dhīmatām" ("the time of the wise passes in the delight of poetics and letters") testifies to the irresistible attraction this subject holds.

In the case of Artha-Brahman (Brahman as meaning/substance), illustrations such as the rope mistaken for a snake seem to suggest its transience and its unfitness for worship. But Shabda-Brahman is ever fit for worship, and so even yogis adore it alongside words such as 'tat sat' and 'tattvamasi'. Hence it is established that Kavya-shastra and Shabda-Brahman are one and the same, merely synonyms.

The principal etymology of the word 'Kavya' is this: it derives from 'kena' (by Brahman) and 'āvyam' (that which is to be protected, attained, or illumined) — that is, Kavya; here the root 'ava' carries the senses of motion, radiance, and protection. Or, it may mean that which is to be worn 'ke' (upon the head). Or, it may mean that the poet (kavi) is one born 'kavau' (in the Supreme Brahman), for indeed the Shrutis give the Supreme Self the name 'kaviḥ svayambhūḥ paribhūḥ'. Or, a kavi is one who weaves cloth in water (ke). Or again, following the root 'kavṛ varṇane' (to describe), a kavi is one who describes even an ordinary object in an extraordinary way, or one who is a seer of what is beyond the ordinary (krāntadarśī).

Since it is composed by a kavi (poet), it is the Kavya of the kavi. Or, 'kavyam' refers to the food and other offerings given with reverence to the departed ancestors dwelling in heaven; in the same way, that which is offered with reverence to the ancient great poets such as Sri Kalidasa is also called Kavya. Thus this Shabda-Brahman, called by the many-meaning name Kavya, is of two kinds. The first — taking refuge in the mouths of the great sages, assuming written form, and remaining fixed permanently in one place like the water of wells, springs, and ponds — accomplishes all the world's affairs through names such as the Vedas. The second — arising in the mind of the one in the form of a poet, like 'Shatarupa' (she of a hundred forms), truly assuming hundreds of forms, and ever shining like the sun and moon — is that renowned by the name 'Kavya'. Just as the son of Shiva the Conqueror of Death (Kumaraswami), wishing to conquer the six directions, united his six faces as if into a single lotus, so too the wise well know that this Kavya proceeds with an eye toward six purposes.

"kāvyaṃ yaśase'rthakṛte vyavahāravide śivetarakṣataye |

sadyaḥ paranirvṛtaye kāntāsammitatayopadeśayuje" —

(Kavya bestows fame, wealth, and knowledge of worldly affairs; it destroys inauspiciousness; it grants immediate bliss of Brahman; and it instructs pleasantly, as a beloved wife does). It is precisely because of these purposes that scholars take such interest in the composition of Kavya. As the saying goes, "even a fool does not undertake any task without some purpose in mind" — how much greater, then, is the delight of the discerning in a task that yields two fruits at once. We hear it said in the world that "a certain sage, holding his water-pot and darbha grass, pours water at the foot of a mango tree; by that water the mango tree is nourished, and the ancestors are satisfied — thus a single act accomplishes two purposes." But this thing called Kavya is soft as fresh butter, and bestows many fruits at once. It is for this very reason that great poets have fashioned many a Kavya-body, free from the fears of old age and death. Among these, the Mahakavya "Kumarasambhavam," composed by Sri Kalidasa, telling the story of Kumaraswami, the son of the Lord, has long adorned the faces of the learned as an ornament.

As I write these very lines, a joyous wish, too, arose fortunately in my own heart — namely, that if scholars take such delight in the Kavya of the younger son, Kumaraswami, then surely a Kavya composed upon the elder Lord Ganapati would without fail captivate the minds of the learned. Moreover, while people know Kumaraswami only a little, Ganapati is renowned to one and all, from the smallest child to the eldest elder. Even a boy ploughing a field drives his plough while uttering Ganapati's name; and he holds a place among the five principal deities. By the very custom of saying "śrī gaṇeśaḥ kṛtaḥ" (the auspicious mark of Ganesha has been made) at the outset of every undertaking, his very name shines as synonymous with beginnings. Having considered all this, I set out, to the best of my humble ability, to worship that Lord in this way. I therefore earnestly and humbly beg you to examine this entire work and, by granting your consent, bring this effort of mine to fruition.

If any faults natural to human frailty should appear anywhere in this work, I fold my lotus-like hands and beg that you kindly bring them to my notice. And should you, engaged in boundless undertakings, be unable to examine this entire work, I firmly believe that you will at least examine it after the manner of 'shalākā-parīkṣā' (piercing a book with a needle to sample a page) or 'sthālīpulāka-nyāya' (judging whether all the rice is cooked by testing a single grain). Whichever great souls read this work and, with a gracious heart, bestow their blessings upon it, I close by expressing my gratitude for their causeless compassion, acknowledging my great debt to them.

"āparitoṣād vidhuṣāṃ na sādhu manye prayoga vijñānam" (I do not consider my endeavor a success until the learned themselves are fully satisfied).

— Prabhudatta Shastri

title: Opinion of Archana Prakashan publishers, Nagpur
html:
Opinion of Archana Prakashan publishers, Nagpur

This is a matter of the highest fortune for the world of Sanskrit, for scholars capable of composing such Mahakavyas still exist even in this present age. Mahakavyas of this kind were once composed even before the invasions of foreign powers. Perhaps no one has come across another Mahakavya written in the tradition of Kalidasa, the preceptor among poets, and his 'Kumara Sambhavam'. Indeed, it was that very Mahakavya, 'Kumara Sambhava', that kindled the desire to compose this 'Ganapati Sambhava'. A younger brother such as Kumaraswami could only rejoice at receiving a Kavya that glorifies the fame of his elder brother, could he not? Thus, even greater foresight was shown in the choice of subject for this Kavya than in its actual composition.

The beauty of this Kavya is increased fourfold by the very names given to its sargas (cantos). The other matters contained within it will become known simply by reading the table of contents; nevertheless, we offer you here some indication of what captivated us and led us to undertake its publication:

(1) 'Himagiri Parichayamu' (Introduction to the Himalayas) — Here, the description of Kashmir, the very chest of today's Himalayas, and of Nepal, its head, is well worth beholding. The parallel drawn between Kashmir and the Indian national flag, and the very form of the Indian soldiers who stand guard upon the Himalayas, are memorable indeed. The advertisement, as it were, of their saffron and musk, is composed with great wit, without need of any agent. The blessed sight of Amarnath and Pashupatinath is made available here, right at home.

(2) 'Girisha Girija Panigrahanamu' (The Wedding of Shiva and Parvati) — Here, the splendor of marriage in the Indian tradition, the names of Shiva's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and the farewell (vidaayi) of Parvati Devi, are most joyous to behold.

(3) 'Yogashakti Chamatkriti' (The Wonder of Yogic Power) — This shows both Shiva's yogic worship and the manner in which Parvati Devi's yogic power bore fruit upon the son she made of clay.

(4) 'Shastraartha Shastribeevamu' (The Debate, and Its Turn to Arms) — The debate (Shastrartha) that Shiva conducts with his own son on the question of fatherhood, and its astonishing transformation thereafter into a matter of arms, is a marvel of craft.

(5) 'Gajamanujayojanamu' (The Union of Elephant and Man) — Here lies the secret of how an elephant and a human being come to stand joined as one, along with the praise of the scholars of Kashi.

(6) Tanaikadanta Prasangah (The Episode of the Single Tusk) — The story of how Ganesha's tusk was broken by Parashurama is most instructive.

(7) 'Mahabharata Lekhakhyanamu' (The Tale of the Writing of the Mahabharata) — We have all heard of this before, but the manner in which that writing actually took place may be seen here for the very first time.

(8) 'Devamodakopaharamu' (The Divine Offering of the Modaka) — The tales of how the modaka (sweet dumpling) came to be connected with Ganesha are sweeter still than the modaka itself.

(9) 'Ganashasanamu' (The Rule of the Ganas) — The thorough exposition of its characteristics, its methods, and the means to its stability is well worth the attention of today's masters of statecraft.

(10) 'Kavyantara Pushparpanamu' (An Offering of Flowers from His Other Works) — Here the poet has given, in a most delightful manner, samples of his other compositions along with an account of his own life.

Other matters — such as the birth of a daughter to the Himalaya mountain, the images of reconciliation set up on Kailasa and other such virtuous themes, the simplicity of meditative samadhi, and passages on devotion to the motherland that draw one toward the many unattained benefits of education — are exceedingly delightful.

It is a widely held view that the publication of Sanskrit Mahakavyas is not an encouraging prospect from a financial standpoint. For this very reason, this Mahakavya had not come to light for many years. It is only in the hope that the scholarly community of India will surely embrace such a work that this venture in publishing has been undertaken. Had it remained unpublished, it stood in danger of being lost to time altogether — and the loss of such a Kavya would have been a matter of grief to us all.

We do not merely hope that this endeavor of ours will succeed — we hold full confidence in it, and confidence too that we shall bring to light still more unpublished works belonging to the Sanskrit language.

The Publishers.
